issues.legal_issue: The High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction does not permit it to reappraise evidence and replace a reasonable factual finding of a subordinate court.
material_facts: The trial court and the appellate bench of the subordinate court considered the evidence and found that the obstructionist was in possession as a licensee on the relevant date.
The courts differed on aspects of the evidence, and the appellate bench’s conclusion was one of the factual views the evidence could support.
The High Court reassessed the evidence and displaced the appellate bench’s finding without establishing that it was perverse or otherwise affected by a legal error.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 227 by preferring its own view of the evidence over a reasonable factual finding supported by the record.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 confers supervisory, not appellate, jurisdiction. A High Court should not reappraise evidence or disturb a finding within the subordinate court’s jurisdiction unless, for example, the finding is perverse, unsupported by material evidence, affected by a misdirection in law, contrary to the preponderance of evidence, or results in manifest injustice. The Court relied on D.N. Banerji v. P.R. Mukharjee, Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte, Warryam Singh v. Amarnath, Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division, Harbans Lal v. Jagmohan Saran, Trimbak Gangadhar Telang v. Ram Chandra Ganesh Bhide, and Smt. M.M. Amonkar v. Dr. S.A. Johari; it also referred to R. v. Northumberland Compensation Appeal Tribunal, Ex parte Shaw, on the limits of certiorari and supervisory review.

rule.if: article_227_supervisory_review and lower_finding_based_on_material_evidence and lower_finding_is_a_reasonable_view and not legal_misdirection and not manifest_injustice

predicates.article_227_supervisory_review: The proceeding asks a High Court to exercise supervisory jurisdiction over a subordinate court’s factual finding.
predicates.lower_finding_based_on_material_evidence: The subordinate court reached its finding on evidence in the record.
predicates.lower_finding_is_a_reasonable_view: The evidence permits the subordinate court’s finding as a reasonable view of the facts.
predicates.legal_misdirection: The subordinate court’s finding resulted from a misdirection in law.
predicates.manifest_injustice: The subordinate court’s finding resulted in manifest injustice.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a reasonable factual finding supported by evidence, and there is no legal misdirection or manifest injustice, the High Court must leave that finding undisturbed.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant protected by rent-control legislation may grant a licence before an eviction decree, and a licensee in actual occupation on the statutory date may become a deemed tenant despite a contrary contract or a restriction on transferring the tenancy interest.
material_facts: The subordinate appellate court found that the obstructionist had continuously occupied the premises as a licensee from before the statutory date and was in occupation on that date.
The tenant’s eviction decree was passed after the statutory date, so the tenant’s protected tenancy had not ended when the licence was created or on the statutory date.
The licence was created before the statutory date, and the tenant’s original tenancy terms did not specifically authorize the creation of a licence.
issues.conclusion: The licensee was entitled to be treated as a tenant under the Act; a tenant protected by statute could grant a licence before an eviction decree, whether or not the tenancy agreement expressly permitted it.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 15A(1) and 14(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, read together, protect a licensee who was in actual occupation on the statutory date and provide for the licensee to become the landlord’s tenant when the licensor’s tenant interest ends. Section 15(1) restricts later grants of licences, and section 13(1)(e) provides a ground for eviction for unlawful grants after the relevant amendment; those provisions do not defeat the protection for qualifying pre-date licensees. Under sections 52 and 53 of the Indian Easements Act, a licence is a personal privilege, not an interest in property, and its creation is not a transfer of the tenancy interest under section 108(j) of the Transfer of Property Act. A statutorily protected tenant remains in the position of a contractual tenant until an eviction decree is passed and may create a licence before then. The Court relied on Waman Shrinivas Kini v. Ratilal Bhagwandas & Co., V. Dhanapal Chettiar v. Yesodai Ammal, Gian Devi Anand v. Jeevan Kumar, and B.M. Lall v. Dunlop Rubber & Co.; it distinguished Ludhichem Agencies v. Ahmed R.V. Peer Mohamed because the licence there was created after the tenant’s interest had ended. It rejected the restrictive construction adopted by the Bombay High Court Full Bench in Ratanlal Chandiprasad Jalan v. Raniram Darkhan. In construing the overriding words of section 15A, the Court also relied on The South India Corporation (P) Ltd. v. Secretary, Board of Revenue, Aswini Kumar Ghosh v. Arabinda Bose, Dominion of India v. Shribai A. Irani, Nokes v. Doncaster Amalgamated Collieries, Heydon’s case, and Becks v. Smith.

rule.if: rent_control_licensee_protection_claim and licence_created_before_statutory_cutoff and licensee_in_actual_occupation_on_cutoff and licensor_still_tenant_when_licence_created

predicates.rent_control_licensee_protection_claim: A person seeks tenant protection under rent-control law on the basis of occupation as a licensee.
predicates.licence_created_before_statutory_cutoff: The tenant granted the licence before the statutory cutoff for protection of existing licensees.
predicates.licensee_in_actual_occupation_on_cutoff: The licensee was in actual occupation of the premises on the statutory cutoff date.
predicates.licensor_still_tenant_when_licence_creat: The person granting the licence remained a protected tenant and had not yet been evicted by decree when the licence was created.

issues.definition: A person seeking rent-control protection as a licensee becomes a deemed tenant when the licence was created while the licensor remained a protected tenant and the licensee was in actual occupation on the statutory cutoff date.
